chunk_findings.detail:
`addenda` deliberately drops inbound `related` links whose source already appears as the target of one of the record's own outbound `related` links:

```python
out_related = {x["target"] for x in links if x["relation"] == "related"}
...
if x["relation"] == "related" and src in out_related:
    continue  # the back-link already listed it
```

That is fine for *display* (`show` still lists the pair once via the back-link), but `new_reports` derives its count **only** from `addenda(...)["linked_from"]` plus additions:

```python
linked = [x for x in a["linked_from"] if _epoch(x["at"]) >= since]
return {"count": len(adds) + len(linked), ...}
```

So any report filed against an item as a `related` link is invisible to the count. Concrete input: item X is claimed at time T. Afterwards a new record R is filed with a `related` link to X. Per the docstring in `addenda` ("only `related` also writes a back-link"), this also writes the back-link X→R. Now `addenda(X)` computes `out_related = {R}`, skips the inbound R→X entry, and `new_reports(X, since=T)` returns `count == 0` even though a new report against X exists. This directly contradicts `new_reports`'s own docstring ("The additions **and inbound links** on `rid` made at or after `since`") and the acceptance criterion that the brief "leads with the count", so the brief will under-report `related` additions to a claimed item.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting.py — `addenda` (the `src in out_related` dedup) / `new_reports`

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `addenda_lines` helper is invoked with two structurally different arguments, so at least one of the two call sites is wrong. In `show` (around line 172) it is given the already-selected render value:

```python
extra = addenda_lines(out.data["_render"]["addenda"])
```

while in the brief builder (around line 206) it is given the whole item dict `b` — the same dict that the two preceding lines read as `b["lesson"]` and `b["summary"]`:

```python
lines += addenda_lines(b)
```

These two shapes cannot both be the expected parameter of the same function. If `addenda_lines` expects the addenda value (which is what the `show` call passes), then for any item the brief builder will call it with the item dict instead of `b["addenda"]`/`b["_render"]["addenda"]`; because the brief path uses `lines += addenda_lines(b)` without an `if extra:` guard (unlike `show`), a `None`/wrong-type return raises at that `+=` or silently appends nothing, so the brief never surfaces the new reports it is supposed to lead with. Concretely, take any item that has addenda: `show <bug>` prints them (line 172 path), but the brief for the same item either raises or omits them because `b` is not the addenda object. If instead the brief is correct and `addenda_lines` expects the containing dict, then the `show` call at line 172 passes the sub-value and fails the same way. The two call sites need to agree on one argument contract.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/reporting.py:172 and ddflow/surfaces/commands/reporting.py:206 (`addenda_lines` call sites)

chunk_findings.detail: The `reserve` mechanism is supposed to keep "the whole stays inside the budget", but the floor `max(1, …)` only prevents a negative budget — it does not bound the block that is prepended. `new_reports_block` (same file, just above) can emit up to `_REPORTS_SHOWN` (5) reports of `_REPORT_CAP` (400) chars each, i.e. ~2000 chars ≈ 500 tokens, plus the header and the "N more" line. When the caller passes a `reserve` that is ≥ `cfg.session.brief_max_tokens` (e.g. `session.brief_max_tokens = 300`, a claimed item with 5 new reports → caller's `reserve ≈ 500`), `budget` collapses to `1`, the recovery/lessons text is truncated to `text[:4]`, yet the ~500-token report block is still prepended verbatim. The assembled brief is then ~500 tokens against a 300-token budget, so the acceptance criterion "brief stays within its token budget" is violated exactly in the case the reserve was added to handle. The block itself needs to be clipped/skipped against `cfg.session.brief_max_tokens` rather than relying on the subtraction, which can only shrink the part below it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py:603 (`budget = max(1, cfg.session.brief_max_tokens - reserve)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test runs 40 `lesson add` commands but never asserts their exit status. If the command fails (e.g., because of an invalid argument, a CLI regression, or an environment issue), the lessons are simply not added, yet the test can still pass: the count of new reports remains 30 and the `approx_tokens` value is lower, so the budget assertion `data["approx_tokens"] <= 1200 * 1.1` is trivially satisfied. The test therefore does not actually verify that the brief stays within budget when many lessons compete for space, defeating the purpose of the budget check.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_addenda_render.py:test_brief_with_many_reports_stays_within_its_budget

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent requires `show` to display additions with verbatim text, who, when, and score. The text test asserts `"by reporter"` and `"0.61"` but never checks that a timestamp (the “when” field) is present. The JSON test checks only `text` and `who` for the addition, omitting `when` and `score` entirely. An implementation that accidentally drops the timestamp (or, in the JSON case, the score) would still pass these tests, so the tests do not verify the full set of addition fields required by the change.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff adds two calls to `addenda_lines`, but they pass different things. In the show path it is called as `addenda_lines(out.data["_render"]["addenda"])`, i.e. it navigates *into* `_render` to the `"addenda"` value and passes that value directly. In `_brief_item` it is called as `addenda_lines(b)`, where `b` is the item record that the surrounding lines read via `b["lesson"]` and `b["summary"]` (`if b["lesson"]:`, `lines += ["", b["summary"]]`). A dict with `lesson`/`summary` keys is not the addenda collection that the show call handes over. If `addenda_lines` treats its argument as the list of addenda entries (which the plural name and the `"\n".join(extra)` at the show site imply), then `_brief_item` feeds it a mapping: the function will iterate the dict's string keys and then index them as addenda records, raising a `TypeError`/misrendering for every item, so the brief never prints the additions the acceptance requires. Conversely, if `addenda_lines` expects a record that it reads `.get("addenda")` from, then the show path — which already drilled down to `["addenda"]` — is the wrong one. The two new call sites cannot both be correct as written.

chunk_findings.detail: `new_reports_block` bounds the prepended block only with hardcoded constants—`_REPORTS_SHOWN = 5` and `_REPORT_CAP = 400`—so the block can reach roughly 5×400 characters (≈500 tokens) plus header, independent of `cfg.session.brief_max_tokens`. The `reserve` mechanism does not cap the block; it only shrinks the *body* budget via `budget = max(1, cfg.session.brief_max_tokens - reserve)`. Whenever the block alone is at or above the budget, this fails: e.g. with `session.brief_max_tokens = 120` and a claimed item carrying 5 additions of 400 chars each, the caller computes `reserve ≈ 500`, so `budget = max(1, 120 - 500) = 1`; the body then trips `_approx_tokens(text) > 1` and is cut with `text[: budget * 4]` = `text[:4]`, which (no newline in the first 4 chars) rslits to `""`, leaving only the truncation footer. The returned brief is the ~500-token prepended block plus footer—about 4× over the 120-token budget—while *all* session content is discarded. So the acceptance criterion "brief stays within its token budget" is violated, and the added comment claiming reserve keeps "the whole ... inside the budget" is false precisely whenever the new-reports block alone exceeds `brief_max_tokens`. The `max(1, ...)` silently masks this instead of clamping/reducing the block (e.g. dropping reports or tightening `_REPORTS_SHOWN`/`_REPORT_CAP` against the actual budget).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py: new_reports_block / brief(..., reserve=...)

chunk_findings.detail: The scheme these tests rely on is "count what arrived **since you claimed**", i.e. the implementation must order the pre-claim addition (`"added BEFORE the claim"`) against the claim event, and the two post-claim events (`ADD1` and bug `B2`) against it. The test appends those events through separate processes (`run_cli(proj, "claim", ...)` is a subprocess) and in-process `EventLog.append` calls that execute milliseconds apart, yet never pins a timestamp and never sleeps; correctness depends entirely on the wall clock advancing between the claim write and the following appends. On any run where the log's timestamp has coarser resolution than that gap (classic example: the Windows system clock, which Python's `datetime.now()` only refreshes every ~15.6 ms, or any storage that truncates to seconds), the post-claim `ADD1`/`B2` events tie with the claim. The comparison then either excludes the genuinely-new reports (count 0, failing `text.startswith("## 2 new reports on your item since you claimed")` at the brief assertion and the `"2 new reports on P1.T1 since you claimed"` assertions in `test_heartbeat_and_gate_status_mention_the_count`), or, if at-or-after semantics are used, the pre-claim addition ties too and is included as well (count 3), so `assert "added BEFORE the claim" not in text` also fails. The same boundary is exercised in `test_a_related_record_filed_after_the_claim_is_counted`, which expects exactly `"## 1 new report"` from events written immediately after the claim. A deterministic test would inject/log an explicit claim timestamp for the reports to be compared against (or sleep past the clock granularity) rather than depending on two near-simultaneous wall-clock reads being distinguishable.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_addenda_render.py `_claimed_with_reports` / `test_brief_for_a_claimed_item_leads_with_the_count_and_the_reports` / `test_a_related_record_filed_after_the_claim_is_counted`

chunk_findings.detail:
The new count is attached to only one of heartbeat's two return paths. The `O.ok("lease.renewed", renewed=True, waiters=..., globs_withheld=..., new_reports=_new_report_count(st, item))` return carries the field, but the very next `O.nothing("lease.renewed", ...)` return — the no-op path a still-valid lease takes when renewal isn't due yet — does not. So for the common heartbeat case (agent already holds a valid lease and heartbeats within the interval), `_new_report_count` is never called and the count is never surfaced, even though the stated acceptance is "`ddflow heartbeat` … carries the count in one line" and the agent is precisely the holder who should be told "N new reports on your item since you claimed." Concrete scenario: agent A claims item X at T0; a new report lands at T1; A calls `ddflow heartbeat X` before the renewal threshold and gets the `O.nothing` outcome with no `new_reports` field, so it is never nudged. Either route `_new_report_count` into both returns, or move the computation before the branch and pass it to whichever outcome is returned.

(Everything else in this hunk — the `lease is None`/`lease` guards, `acquired_at` as the since-timestamp, and the reserve/cap arithmetic in `brief` — is consistent: the block is capped at `brief_max_tokens * 4 // 2` chars, and `reserve = _approx_tokens(reports_block)` keeps the block+body within the same token measure the brief itself uses.)
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py — heartbeat (`new_reports` only on the O.ok renewal path)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py — heartbeat (`new_reports` only on the O.ok renewal path)

chunk_findings.detail: The new `reserve` parameter is documented as making “the whole stay inside the budget”, but the function only bounds the body it returns; it never bounds the prepended new-reports block, and the `max(1, ...)` clamp silently collapses the body instead of preventing the overflow. Whenever the caller’s `reserve` (the token size of `new_reports_block(...)`) is ≥ `cfg.session.brief_max_tokens`, `budget` becomes 1, the body is truncated to ~1 token, and the concatenation the caller forms is still ≈ `reserve` tokens — larger than the configured budget. `new_reports_block` can easily reach this size: `_REPORTS_SHOWN` (5) × `_REPORT_CAP` (400) chars plus headers is >500 tokens. Concretely, with `session.brief_max_tokens = 400` and a claimed item carrying five 400-char additions, `new_reports_block` yields ≈540 tokens, the caller passes `reserve ≈ 540`, `budget = max(1, 400-540) = 1`, the base brief is cut to almost nothing, and the final brief is ≈540 tokens — still over the 400-token budget the acceptance criterion requires. The body needs to stop shrinking (or the block needs to be elided) once `reserve >= brief_max_tokens`, otherwise the change fails its own “brief stays within its token budget” requirement.
chunk_findings.title: `_brief` (`budget = max(1, cfg.session.brief_max_tokens - reserve)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The helper `_addition` sleeps only 10 ms before appending, and several tests append records immediately after `run_cli(... "claim" ...)` without any sleep (`test_a_related_record_filed_after_the_claim_is_counted` lines 150–153, `test_a_lesson_or_decision_linked_to_a_claimed_item_renders_in_the_brief` lines 171–182). On a platform whose wall clock has granularity coarser than 10 ms (Windows ~15.6 ms; some CI/VM clocks 1 s), the claim event and the subsequent record can receive identical timestamps. Because the brief must exclude pre-claim additions, its filter either uses strict `>` (then the new report is dropped: `test_a_related_record_filed_after_the_claim_is_counted` sees 0 instead of “## 1 new report”, and `test_brief_for_a_claimed_item_leads_with_the_count_and_the_reports` sees 1 instead of 2) or `>=` (then “added BEFORE the claim” is included, failing that same brief test). The comment “past the claim’s timestamp on any clock granularity” is false.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_addenda_render.py:38 (`_addition`) / `test_a_related_record_filed_after_the_claim_is_counted`

chunk_findings.detail:
`new_reports` documents itself as returning "the additions and inbound links on `rid`", and the `linked` list is correctly seeded only from `a["linked_from"]` (inbound). But the extra loop then adds *every* entry of `a["links"]` whose relation is `related`. `a["links"]` is `st.links[rid]`, i.e. rid's *own* link set, and per `addenda`'s own comment a new record that is filed `related` to something stores that link **on itself** (State only additionally writes a back-link on the target). So an outbound `related` link that rid filed toward another record is counted as a report *on rid*, attributed to the target (`"record": x["target"]`), even though rid is the author, not the recipient.

Every other relation is asymmetric and correct: an `extends`/`duplicate_of` link only ever shows up as a report on its target (via `linked_from`). `related` is the single relation that is counted on both ends, so it inflates a record's count with its own outgoing links.

Concrete input showing the wrong result: item A is claimed at epoch T; afterwards a `related` link A→X is created at T' ≥ T (creating the link on A and a back-link on X). Calling `new_reports(state, A, T)` still enters the loop, sees `x["relation"] == "related"` with `_epoch(x["at"]) >= T`, and appends it, so `count` becomes 1 and the brief for A prints "1 new report on your item since you claimed" naming X — although nothing was reported against A. (For the counterpart X this is correct; the phantom is only on the acting side, and it also eats into the brief's token budget with a non-report.)

chunk_findings.detail: `time.sleep(0.01)` does not guarantee that the new addition is timestamped after the claim on every clock. In `_claimed_with_reports` the pre-claim addition is appended and the claim is recorded immediately afterwards, so on a clock whose resolution is ≥10 ms (e.g. a log that stores whole-second ISO timestamps, or Windows' ~15.6 ms wall-clock tick) the pre-claim addition, the claim, and the post-claim addition can all carry the same timestamp. Then the "since you claimed" filter either excludes the post-claim report (if it compares strictly `>`, giving count 0 instead of the asserted 2 in `test_brief_for_a_claimed_item_leads_with_the_count_and_the_reports`) or includes the pre-claim addition (if it compares `>=`, yielding count 3 and making `"added BEFORE the claim"` appear in the brief, which the test forbids). The same file's own timestamp regex `\d\d:\d\d:\d\d\S* by reporter` even tolerates a second-only timestamp, so this granularity is plausible for the implementation under test. The comment "past the claim's timestamp on any clock granularity" is therefore false; the setup needs an ordering that does not depend on timestamp resolution (sleep well past the resolution, or make the cutoff event-sequence-based).

chunk_findings.detail: The new-reports count relies on `x["source"] == "later"` to re-count the automatic `related` back-link that `addenda` intentionally removes from `linked_from`. But the link records consumed by this change expose only `target`, `relation`, `at`, and `event`; `addenda` derives the owning record from the `st.links` key and stores it under an added `record` field, and reads no `source` field from a link. So for any item with an outbound `related` link (the back-link case the branch exists for), `x["source"]` raises `KeyError: 'source'`, crashing `brief`/`new_reports`; and if such a key were the link's originating-record id, the comparison to the literal `"later"` would always be false and the related report would be dropped from the count. Demonstrated input: a claimed item X plus a newly filed record marked `related` to X.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting.py new_reports (x["source"])

chunk_findings.detail: The first argument to `out.body` is now constructed as `(waiters, f"...wakes them:") + <conditional-expression>`. The conditional expression evaluates to a `str` in *both* branches: when `out.data.get("new_reports")` is truthy it is `"\n" + new_reports_line(...)` (a string), and when it is falsy it is `""` (also a string). Therefore the expression is always `tuple + str`, which raises `TypeError: can only concatenate tuple (not "str") to tuple` — Python does not have a `tuple.__add__` that accepts a string, and there is no list/tuple coercion here. Concretely, the very first invocation of this renewal path (`ddflow lifecycle renew ...`, i.e. the "waiters on your item" heartbeat branch) crashes before `out.body` is even called, regardless of whether `new_reports` is 0 or nonzero; even the intended "no new reports" case fails because `()+ ""` is a TypeError. The intended fix is to make the added element a one-element tuple, e.g. `(...) + (("\n" + new_reports_line(...)) if out.data.get("new_reports") else "",)`, or to build the message as a list.
